record.paper_title: Evolutionary Dynamics of Cancer: From Epigenetic Regulation to Cell Population Dynamics—Mathematical Model Framework, Applications, and Open Problems
record.context_brief: Entropy production and dissipation in epigenetically heterogeneous cell populations
record.original_question: Consider the same delay-free heterogeneous stem-cell regeneration model with total cell number Q(t)=∫Ω Q(t,x)dx, epigenetic-state fraction f(t,x)=Q(t,x)/Q(t), and multicellular entropy E(t)=−∫Ω f(t,x)log f(t,x)dx. For the induced dynamics of f(t,x), can the entropy derivative dE/dt be decomposed as epr−edr, where both the entropy production rate epr and the entropy dissipation rate edr are always nonnegative? More broadly, under what conditions on the rate functions and the nonlocal epigenetic transition probability p(x,y) is tissue development, and in particular cancer development, an entropy-increasing process?

evidence.quote: Let Q(t) = ∫Ω Q(t,x) for the total cell number at time t, and f(t,x) = Q(t,x) / Q(t) for the fraction of cells with given epigenetic state x. The entropy of the multicellular system at time t is deﬁned as E(t) = − ∫Ω f(t,x) log f(t,x)dx.

The entropy problem asks: how can we decompose the rate of entropy change into entropy production rate (epr) and entropy dissipate rate (edr) so that dE / dt = epr − edr, and both epr and edr are alway non-negative.

Solutions to this problem is essential to answer the question of how the entropy change along the process of tissue development. In particular, is cancer development a process of entropy increasing[15, 42]?
For the general situation, it is not know how the entropy production rate and dissipation rate should be deﬁned, and under which situation the development process is entropy increasing.

artifact.category_tag: entropy production in nonlocal population dynamics
artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let Ω ⊂ ℝ^d be a measurable space of epigenetic states. Consider a heterogeneous cell population whose density Q(t,x) ≥ 0 over states x ∈ Ω evolves according to a delay-free stem-cell regeneration model of the form

   ∂_t Q(t,x) = -(β(x) + μ(x)) Q(t,x) + 2 ∫_Ω β(y) p(x,y) Q(t,y) dy,

where β(x) ≥ 0 is the proliferation rate, μ(x) ≥ 0 is the apoptosis/removal rate, and p(x,y) ≥ 0 is a nonlocal epigenetic transition kernel satisfying ∫_Ω p(x,y) dx = 1 for every y ∈ Ω (so that each dividing cell at state y produces two daughters whose epigenetic states are distributed according to p(·,y)).

Define the total cell number
   Q(t) = ∫_Ω Q(t,x) dx,
the epigenetic-state fraction
   f(t,x) = Q(t,x) / Q(t),
and the multicellular Gibbs–Shannon entropy
   E(t) = - ∫_Ω f(t,x) log f(t,x) dx.

Derive the induced evolution equation for f(t,x), and address the following questions.

(a) Can the time derivative dE/dt be decomposed as
   dE/dt = epr(t) - edr(t),
where epr(t) ≥ 0 (entropy production rate) and edr(t) ≥ 0 (entropy dissipation rate) are functionals of f, β, μ, p that are pointwise (in t) nonnegative for every admissible state f?

(b) Provide explicit formulas for epr and edr in this decomposition, and characterize the conditions on the rate functions β, μ and on the nonlocal transition kernel p(x,y) under which the developmental process is entropy-increasing, i.e. dE/dt ≥ 0 for all t ≥ 0.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem in the framework of multicellular entropy for heterogeneous stem-cell regeneration models. No published general decomposition of dE/dt into nonnegative entropy production and dissipation rates, nor a general characterization of when tissue/cancer development is entropy-increasing, appears to be available; the problem is stated to remain open in the general setting.

status_evidence.title: Evolutionary Dynamics of Cancer: From Epigenetic Regulation to Cell Population Dynamics
status_evidence.snippet: For the general situation, it is not known how the entropy production rate and dissipation rate should be defined, and under which situation the development process is entropy increasing.
status_evidence.claim: The decomposition and characterization are stated as unresolved in general.
